By the end of this lecture, you will be able to…

items: 1Identify the roles of enzymes in metabolism — how enzymes act as the basic catalytic units of every metabolic pathway.
2Understand the principles of metabolic pathways — irreversibility, the first committed step, regulation, and cellular localisation.
3Understand the major metabolic control mechanisms — control of enzyme levels, enzyme activity, compartmentation, and hormonal regulation.

blocks.x: Core definitions
Metabolic pathway A series of connected enzymatic reactions that produce a specific product. It consists of sequential steps, with over 2,000 reactions catalysed by distinct enzymes.
Metabolite Enzymes are the basic units of metabolism; the substrates of these enzymes are called metabolites.
Metabolon Soluble enzymes are organised into ultra-structures in the cell, where consecutively acting enzymes are associated with multiple enzyme complexes called metabolons.

Temporary structural-functional complexes usually form between sequential enzymes of a metabolic pathway, held together by non-covalent interactions, and structural elements of the cell such as integral membrane proteins and cytoskeletal proteins.
How enzymes are organised in a pathway
Substrate→ E1→ E2→ E3→ E4→ Product

Enzymes may be physically separated (metabolites diffuse between active sites), form a multi-enzyme complex (metabolites pass directly between active sites), or reside within a membrane (enzyme and substrate diffuse in two dimensions).
Three shapes of metabolic pathways

c: Series of independent enzymes; the product of one reaction is the substrate for the next.
Intermediates (e.g. oxaloacetate) are regenerated every turn. Very few pathways are cyclic.
The same set of enzymes is used repeatedly in polymerisation reactions.

blocks.x: Introduction & foundational rules
Every metabolic pathway — however many reactions it contains — obeys the same four organising principles.
Metabolic pathways are irreversible

Metabolic pathways are highly exergonic, which gives the pathway direction. Hence, if two metabolites are interconvertible, the pathway from the first to the second must differ from the reverse pathway, allowing the two pathways to be independently regulated.
Every pathway has a first committed step

Most reactions in a metabolic pathway are near equilibrium. However, every pathway has an irreversible reaction committing the intermediate it produces to continue down the pathway. Beyond this committed step, the reaction proceeds to completion.
All metabolic pathways are regulated
Control of the metabolic flux of metabolites through a pathway is accomplished by regulating the rate-determining step of the pathway, which often is the first committed step.
Pathways occur in specific cellular locations

Eukaryotes use organelles to compartmentalise metabolic pathways, allowing different pathways to occur in specific locations and permitting independent regulation — e.g. mitochondria, cytosol, nucleus.
Organelles and their metabolic pathways

c: Replication of DNA; synthesis of tRNA, mRNA and some nuclear proteins
Lipid synthesis; direction of biosynthetic products to their ultimate location
Amino acid oxidation; catalase and peroxidase reactions; sterol degradation; in plants, glyoxylate cycle reactions
Maturation of glycoproteins and other components of membranes and secretory vessels
Citric acid cycle; electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation; fatty acid oxidation; amino acid catabolism; pyruvate oxidation
Segregation of hydrolytic enzymes such as ribonuclease and acid phosphatase
Glycolysis; many reactions in gluconeogenesis; pentose phosphate pathway; activation of amino acids; fatty acid synthesis; nucleotide synthesis

blocks.x: Reaction chemistry
Nearly every step in every pathway falls into one of six reaction classes, each catalysed by its own family of enzymes.
Class 1
Crucial to many pathways — valuable energy is often derived from oxidising carbon compounds. Catalysed by oxidoreductases or dehydrogenases.
Example: succinate dehydrogenase removes two hydrogen atoms from succinate, reducing FAD to FADH₂ as succinate is oxidised to fumarate — a step of the citric acid cycle.
Class 2
Form bonds using free energy released from ATP cleavage. Catalysed by synthases or ligases.
Example: pyruvate + CO₂ + ATP + H₂O ⇌ oxaloacetate + ADP + Pi + H⁺ — the ATP-dependent formation of a carbon–carbon bond that combines smaller molecules into larger ones.
Class 3
Rearrange atoms within a molecule, preparing it for subsequent reactions such as oxidation-reduction. Catalysed by isomerases or epimerases.
Example: aconitase converts citrate → cis-aconitate → isocitrate, moving the hydroxyl group of citrate from a tertiary to a secondary position so it can be oxidised and decarboxylated.
Class 4
A functional group is transferred from an activated carrier to an acceptor. Catalysed by transferases.
Example: hexokinase transfers a phosphoryl group from ATP to glucose, forming glucose-6-phosphate and trapping glucose in the cell so further catabolism can occur.
Class 5
Cleave bonds by adding water, breaking down large molecules to facilitate further metabolism or reuse components for biosynthesis. Catalysed by hydrolases.
Example: sucrose + H₂O → glucose + fructose. Proteins are similarly digested by hydrolytic cleavage.

items.title: Addition/removal of groups at double bonds

blocks.x: Class 6
Functional groups are added to double bonds, or removed to form double bonds. Catalysed by lyases (bond cleavage) or by dehydration.

Examples: aldolase splits fructose 1,6-bisphosphate into dihydroxyacetone phosphate + glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate; enolase dehydrates 2-phosphoglycerate to phosphoenolpyruvate, setting up the next group-transfer step that forms ATP.
Reaction class → enzyme family
Regulation
Cells regulate metabolic flux through four complementary strategies: how much enzyme is made, how active it is, where it works, and what hormones tell it to do.
Control of enzyme levels

The level of a single enzyme varies under different environmental conditions, primarily because of variations in the enzyme's rate of synthesis — a phenomenon particularly well understood in bacteria. When a usable substrate is added to a bacterial growth medium, the abundance of enzymes needed to process it may increase by synthesising new proteins, from less than one molecule per cell to thousands of molecules per cell. This is called enzyme induction.
Lactose absent: the active repressor protein binds to the operator. RNA polymerase cannot attach to the promoter, so the operon is turned off and the lactose-processing genes are not transcribed.

Lactose present: lactose inactivates the repressor protein. RNA polymerase can now bind the promoter and transcribe the lactose-processing genes into mRNA, which is translated into the enzymes needed for lactose processing.
Control of enzyme activity
The catalytic activity of an existing enzyme can be controlled in two ways:

The ligand can be a substrate, product, or allosteric effector. Allosteric activation or inhibition usually acts on the committed step of a pathway: effectors bind specific regulatory sites, altering subunit–subunit interactions within the enzyme and thereby controlling product formation. Allosteric inhibitors distort the active site so substrate cannot bind productively; allosteric activators restore/open the active site so substrate binds and is converted.

Mainly through phosphorylation of serine, threonine or tyrosine residues. More complex covalent regulation involves adenylation (transfer of the adenylate moiety of ATP) and ADP-ribosylation (transfer of the ADP-ribosyl moiety from NAD⁺).
Compartmentation

In eukaryotic cells, enzymes participating in the same process are localised to a particular compartment. For example, RNA polymerases are found in the nucleus, where DNA transcription to RNA occurs; enzymes of the electron transport system and oxidative phosphorylation are all found in the mitochondria. The regulatory function of compartmentation arises from the selective permeability of membranes to metabolites, which controls the passage of intermediates from one compartment to another.
Compartmentation in glucose metabolism
Glucose (cytosol)→ Glycolysis → Pyruvate (cytosol)→ Acetyl-CoA (mitochondria)→ Citric acid cycle + oxidative phosphorylation (mitochondria)→ ATP, H₂O, CO₂

Glycolysis produces ATP and NADH in the cytosol; pyruvate then crosses into the mitochondrion, where the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation consume O₂ and generate the bulk of the cell's ATP, releasing CO₂ and H₂O.
Hormonal regulation
Hormones are substances synthesised by specialised cells and circulated through the blood to remote target cells. There are two types of metabolic response to hormones.

With steroid hormones (e.g. oestrogen), the hormone enters the target cell and interacts with an intracellular protein receptor. The resultant hormone–receptor complex migrates to the nucleus, where it binds to specific sites in the genome and either activates or represses the transcription of genes — leading to new mRNA and, via translation at the ribosome, new protein.

items: Steroid hormone diffuses into the cytoplasm and binds its receptor (often released from a receptor–chaperonin complex involving molecular chaperones).
The receptor–hormone complex undergoes phosphorylation and becomes a DNA-associated receptor.
Binding to chromatin drives transcription (mRNA) and then translation (new protein) at the ribosome.

blocks.x: In other hormone responses, an intracellular second messenger is synthesised to control metabolic reactions. The hormone (first messenger) acts extracellularly by binding to a receptor in the plasma membrane.

items: Nonsteroid hormone binds its membrane receptor.
The receptor's associated G-protein exchanges GDP for GTP.
The GTP-bound complex activates adenylyl cyclase in the membrane.
Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP into the second messenger, cAMP.
cAMP produces the effect on cellular function.

blocks.x: Example: in glycogen mobilisation, the hormone glucagon binds its receptor and activates synthesis of the second messenger cAMP, which in turn results in the breakdown of glycogen.
